   # Mapping the limitations of current AI systems
However, [experts warn](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/international-ai-safety-report-2025/international-ai-safety-report-2025) that they could also pose national security threats if not reliably [aligned](https://alignmentproject.aisi.gov.uk/about) with human intent, as well as having the potential to cause disruptive labour market effects.

Based on these interviews, a literature review, and a workshop with the AISI Research Unit, the report identifies eight limitations of current AI systems, alongside evidence that would indicate progress towards overcoming them.

### Limitations of current AI systems
#### Performance on tasks that are hard to verify
AI systems already perform at the level of human experts in certain verifiable domains in which performance can be easily assessed, such as mathematics and coding, but still struggle with other tasks that would be required for automating most cognitive labour. For example, the consequences of many real-world strategic decisions can take a long time to manifest and are difficult to attribute to particular actions and interventions. Decisions can also require aesthetic or intuitive judgements that are harder to rate objectively.

While current LLMs are, of course, not limited to verifiable domains, performance beyond this is lagging. Evidence of progress could include officially adjudicated wins in competitions that cannot be automatically graded, such as certain essay prizes.

#### Performance in complex environments
In-the-wild evaluations suggest that AI systems currently struggle in these more realistic environments.

#### Reliability
AI systems occasionally make errors, such as [hallucinating](https://openai.com/index/why-language-models-hallucinate/) false information. These errors can decrease willingness to deploy them in high-stakes contexts and can also degrade their performance on long tasks (since small errors in many sequential steps can compound to create larger failures). Not only are AI systems sometimes wrong, but they often appear _confidently_ wrong, suggesting that they lack a high degree of ‘meta-awareness’ about the extent of their own knowledge. They could instead be a result of training objectives that incentivise confident claims, or even of purposeful deception, which has been detected in several frontier models.

These include benchmarks involving long serial reasoning problems ( [RE-Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15114), [HCAST](https://metr.org/hcast.pdf)) and those measuring hallucinations ( [HalluEval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11747), [HalluLens](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.17550), [HHEM](https://www.vectara.com/blog/hhem-2-1-a-better-hallucination-detection-model)).

But for every organization that has successfully deployed [AI](https://www.simplilearn.com/tutorials/artificial-intelligence-tutorial/what-is-artificial-intelligence), there are several that have hit serious roadblocks, or, worse, deployed systems that have caused real harm.

## Regulatory and Strategic Challenges of AI
### 1. Evolving Regulation
Staying current with regulatory changes across markets requires dedicated legal and compliance capacity that most small- and mid-sized AI teams don't have.
